SYNTHETIC TEST MATERIAL
Tom's AUD Study Plan - Fall 2026

Testing window: 8:30 AM check-in, Prometric center, downtown

EXAM DOMAINS AND WEIGHTS (AUD)
Area I - Ethics, Professional Responsibilities and General Principles: 15-25%
  Topics: AICPA Code of Professional Conduct, independence, PCAOB and SEC rules, engagement acceptance, quality management, professional skepticism, responsibilities for fraud and noncompliance with laws.
Area II - Assessing Risk and Developing a Planned Response: 25-35%
  Topics: Planning, understanding the entity and its environment, internal control (COSO), risk of material misstatement, materiality, audit risk model, fraud risk factors, group audits, using the work of specialists and internal auditors.
Area III - Performing Further Procedures and Obtaining Evidence: 30-40%
  Topics: Audit sampling (attribute and variance), substantive analytical procedures, confirmations, inventory observation, estimates, related parties, subsequent events, going concern, written representations, IT audit evidence, SOC reports.
Area IV - Forming Conclusions and Reporting: 10-20%

notes:
AUD notes - Tom - class 3 and 4

TOPIC 1: Audit risk + materiality
AR = RMM x DR (RMM = IR x CR). AR = audit risk, IR = inherent, CR = control risk, DR = detection risk. Auditor can't control IR/CR, only DR. If RMM goes UP -> DR must go DOWN -> more substantive testing, bigger sample, tests closer to YE, more extensive procedures.
- IR = susceptibility of assertion to misstatement before considering controls (complex estimates, cash = high)
- CR = risk that client's ICFR won't prevent/detect misstmt on timely basis
- Overall materiality (OM) = benchmark x %. Ex: 5% of pre-tax income, or 0.5-1% of revenue (for NFP use total expenses/revenue)
- Performance materiality (PM) < OM, cushion for aggregate undetected misstmts
- Clearly trivial threshold = SUM below this don't get accumulated on the SUM schedule
- Materiality is a judgment by the auditor, qualitative factors matter too (fraud, covenants, trends)
- Revise OM if new info comes up during the audit

TOPIC 2: Audit sampling
Stat vs nonstat: stat = random selection + probability theory to eval. Both need judgment on sample size.
Attribute sampling = tests of controls, deviation rate. Key inputs: tolerable deviation rate (TDR), expected deviation rate (EDR), risk of overreliance (ROR). 
- Higher TDR -> smaller sample
- Higher EDR -> LARGER sample
- Higher ROR tolerance -> smaller sample
- Pop size barely matters unless pop is small
If upper deviation limit > TDR -> can't rely on control, assess CR higher.
Variables sampling / MUS (monetary unit sampling) = for substantive tests of balances. MUS good for overstatement, bigger $ items have higher selection chance. Sampling interval = pop book value / sample size. Items > interval are auto selected (top stratum).
Projected misstatement = tainting % x interval. Tainting = misstmt / book value of item.
Sampling risk vs nonsampling risk: sampling risk = conclusion differs from if whole pop tested. Nonsampling = wrong procedure, misread docs, can't be reduced by bigger sample.

TO DO: redo MUS example from ch. 9 (I messed up tainting), ask tutor about CR assessed at max when no testing of controls.
TBS tip: read what's the assertion first!

transcript:
Okay, so, um, let's get started. Welcome back, everybody. Today we're doing audit sampling, and, uh, I know a lot of you are a little scared of this one, but it's really not that bad once you see the pattern. So, let's go.

First thing, what is sampling? Um, audit sampling is applying an audit procedure to less than a hundred percent of the items in a population so that every sampling unit has a chance of being selected. Okay? Every unit has a chance. That's the key phrase. And we use it because, you know, testing everything is just too expensive and, honestly, not necessary.

Now, there are two big flavors. Statistical and nonstatistical. Statistical sampling uses random selection and probability theory to evaluate the results. Nonstatistical, um, you still use judgment, but you don't use the math to measure sampling risk. Both are acceptable under the standards. So don't let a question trick you into thinking one of them is wrong.

Side note, uh, somebody asked me in the hallway if the cafeteria is finally getting that new coffee machine. I have no idea, but I hope so, because the current one is, um, tragic. Okay, back to it.

So, tests of controls use attribute sampling. We're looking for a deviation rate. Is the control working or not? Yes or no. Three inputs matter here. The tolerable deviation rate, the expected deviation rate, and the risk of overreliance. So, um, if the tolerable rate goes up, the sample size goes down, because you're okay with more errors. If the expected deviation rate goes up, the sample size goes up, because you need more evidence to be comfortable. And if you're willing to accept more risk of overreliance, the sample size goes down. I'd write all three of those on a card. This will be on the exam, and it's almost always asked as a direction question, bigger or smaller.

Now, what does population size do? Um, honestly, not much. For large populations it barely changes the sample size. Students always want to say a bigger population needs a bigger sample, and, so, that's the trap.

Okay, substantive testing. Here we're testing dollar balances, so we use either classical variables sampling or monetary unit sampling, MUS. MUS is really popular because larger dollar items have a higher chance of selection. It's great when you're worried about overstatement. The sampling interval is the population book value divided by the sample size. Anything bigger than the interval gets selected automatically, so, um, that's your top stratum, you test it a hundred percent.

For projected misstatement, you take the tainting percentage times the interval. Tainting is the misstatement divided by the book value of the item. So if an item is recorded at a thousand and the right number is eight hundred, tainting is twenty percent. Then multiply by the interval. Simple enough, right? I'll do a full example on the board in a sec.

Now, sampling risk versus nonsampling risk. Sampling risk is the chance your conclusion from the sample is different from what you'd conclude testing the entire population. You can reduce it by increasing the sample size. Nonsampling risk, that's things like using the wrong procedure or misreading a document, and a bigger sample does not fix that. Okay?

Announcement before we finish. The chapter 9 sampling quiz has been scheduled for Wednesday, November 4th, and it will be online, so please make sure you've got a stable connection. Um, and bring a calculator for the practice problems on Monday.

So, let's do the example on the board now. Grab a pen, and, uh, tell me what the interval is if the population is two million and we want a sample of eighty items.
